notes.short: Side by side: Peninnah has children, Hannah has none
notes.about: The verse sets the two wives side by side. Peninnah has children and taunts her rival year after year; Hannah has none, weeps, and takes her grief to the LORD in prayer.

hebrew.note: In Hebrew the two names cross as they do in the BSB: Hannah, Peninnah, then Peninnah, Hannah.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lays the verse out so the two names cross, and the Companion Bible names the figure there. Keil and Delitzsch set the fruitful wife against the childless one, Gill sets Peninnah's children against Hannah's none, and Clarke sums up the chapter: Hannah, being barren, is reproached by Peninnah.
notes.limit: Setting them side by side does not make Hannah faultless: Henry's Concise Commentary says Hannah could not bear the provocation.

cites.quote: a “The name of the one was Hannah, b and the name of the other was Peninnah: b And Peninnah had children, a but Hannah had no children.”
Note the Figure of speech Antimetabole.
Elkanah had two wives, Hannah (grace or gracefulness) and Peninnah (coral), the latter of whom was blessed with children, whereas the first was childless.
Very likely Hannah was his first wife, and having no children by her, he took Peninnah
Hannah, being barren, is reproached by Peninnah, especially in their going up to Shiloh
Hannah could not bear the provocation.
